title: Love people
hook: asked about humaneness, Confucius said: love people (Analects 12.22)
carry: he didn't ask about the horses

segments.voice: Yesterday, upekkha: loving without clinging. Your line was even-hearted. Did you take a breath before steering someone? Today the path moves east, to Chinese voices on love. Day eight hundred fifty.

What does it mean to be humane? A student named Fan Chi put that question to his teacher. Not a question about the stars, or the gods, or how to get ahead. Just the meaning of one word. The teacher was Confucius, and his answer, in plain English, comes to two words. The conversation is in the Analects, a book of his sayings that tradition says his followers gathered. The answer, and the word behind it, is today's lesson.

First, the word. Ren. It's been translated as benevolence, humaneness, goodness, perfect virtue. It's the word Fan Chi asks about in today's passage. Second, the answer. In James Legge's old translation, Fan Chi asked about benevolence, and "The Master said, 'It is to love all men.'" Love people. Not an idea of people: people themselves, starting with the ones in front of you. In the same passage, Fan Chi also asks about knowledge, and the answer matches: know people. Third, a stable fire. The Analects keeps one small scene that shows ren better than a definition. The stables burned while Confucius was away at court. When he came home, he asked whether anyone had been hurt. The text adds that he didn't ask about the horses. His question was about people. Fourth, ren starts close. For Confucius, love grows outward through real relationships: parents, siblings, friends, neighbors, rulers and the ruled. Another saying in the Analects describes the humane person as one who, wanting to stand firm, helps others stand firm too. Love here isn't mainly a feeling. It's a way of treating people, practiced in a household, then a street, then a whole society. Ren is ordinary conduct, done humanely, again and again.
screen: `REN: HUMANENESS.` · `IT IS TO LOVE ALL MEN.` · `HE DIDN'T ASK ABOUT THE HORSES.` · `REN STARTS CLOSE.` · then, large: `LOVE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe slowly. Think back over the last day and find one moment where someone was treated as a means to an end, maybe by you, maybe toward you. A cashier, a coworker, someone on the phone. Don't judge it. Just see it. Then think ahead to today. Choose one person you'll meet, and one small way to treat them humanely: their name, a real question, your full patience. Hold that plan through the sit. The bell holds the time.
Ren. Humaneness in the Analects, which Confucius explained to Fan Chi in plain words: love people. Today's word.
Your line: he didn't ask about the horses. Today, when something goes wrong, ask about the person before you ask about the thing. Day eight hundred fifty.

howItsDone: In Confucian tradition, ren (humaneness) is practiced through everyday relationships: honoring family, keeping faith with friends, and treating others with care.
